title: T
body_md: he robustness of two-level overlapping additive Schwarz (OAS) preconditioners for highly heterogeneous elliptic problems hinges on the choice of the coarse space. We propose an algebraic multiscale (AM) coarse space built from the system matrix alone through an algebraic formulation of the multiscale finite element method (MsFEM). The coarse basis functions are energy-minimizing extensions of the solutions of reduced boundary condition (RBC) problems on the subdomain interface, so that coefficient variations along the interface enter the coarse space. By posing the RBC problems on slabs that extend the interface, the construction also applies to general unstructured domain decompositions. Embedding the AM formulation in an energy-minimizing framework extends it to linear elasticity, and we show that existing condition number bounds for OAS with MsFEM coarse spaces carry over to the algebraic setting. For problems with high coefficient inclusions on the coarse nodes, the AM iteration count and condition number are unaffected by increasing the contrast. In 3D scalar diffusion with log-normal coefficients, AM needs about as many iterations as the generalized Dryja--Smith--Widlund (GDSW) coarse space, while solving a coarse problem ten times smaller. For linear elasticity, omitting the coarse basis functions associated with the rotational rigid body modes yields a fully algebraic coarse space that still scales well for homogeneous problems.

label: lemma:ams_slab_pou
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:ams_slab_pou}
    Let $\Gamma_i \subset \Gamma$ be an edge or a face entity, and let $\Gamma_i'$ be the corresponding slab region. The coarse basis functions $\Phi^{\text{AM}}_{\Gamma_i'}$ computed on $\Gamma_i'$ form a partition of unity, i.e., $\Phi^{\text{AM}}_{\Gamma_i'} \mathbf{1}_{\text{V}} = \mathbf{1}_{\Gamma_i'}$. In addition, the restriction $\Phi^{\text{AM}}_{\Gamma_i}$ of $\Phi^{\text{AM}}_{\Gamma_i'}$ to $\Gamma_i$ forms a partition of unity, i.e., $\Phi^{\text{AM}}_{\Gamma_i} \mathbf{1}_{\text{V}} = \mathbf{1}_{\Gamma_i}$.
